newsitem.title: CHINA: Taiwan groups in HK find red flag a mixed blessing.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan groups in HK find red flag a mixed blessing.

text.p: Pro-Taiwan communities in Hong Kong are adjusting to a new life under communist-ruled China's red flag, with sentiment ranging from dislike to welcome.

"I don't like Hong Kong's return to China because I don't like the Chinese Communist Party. I have more confidence in the British government," said a Taiwan trader in Hong Kong who declined to be identified.
Beijing recovered the territory from London on Monday midnight, ending 156 years of British colonial power.
Hong Kong is home to an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 Taiwanese and thousands of pro-Taiwan people.
Taiwan is China's arch-foe, viewed by Beijing as a rebel province since the Nationalist government fled there after losing the civil war to Communists on the mainland in 1949.
"I have mixed feelings. I am both delighted and worried," said Yum Sin-ling, leader of a pro-Taiwan political party, the One Two Three Democratic Alliance.
"The reversion is a cause for delight," he said. "But I'm worried about a regress in democracy and pressure on freedom of speech," said Yum, who has extensive connections in Taiwan.

The comments came as Taiwan's representative here Koo Chen-fu said Hong Kong's leader Tung Chee-hwa appointed a member of his inner advisory cabinet to act as his intermediary on Taiwan-Hong Kong relations.
Beijing said on Thursday any official contact or exchanges between Taiwan and Hong Kong needed the approval of the central government.
The transfer of rule in Hong Kong has raised fears over a possible dilution of democracy and freedoms.
China scrapped an elected legislature upon the handover and replaced it with an appointed, unelected chamber. Chief Executive Tung has also introduced laws to curb civil rights.
On top of that, Taiwan people in Hong Kong have faced an uncertain post-handover future under the red flag, worrying whether China will take steps to curtail their presence.
Until this year pro-Taiwan communities in Hong Kong have flown Taiwan's "Republic of China" flag with impunity.
Yum said he expected people with Taiwanese background to face some pressure under the new regime.
"We expect to come under some pressure," Yum said. "But there should be no big pressure because that would not help China's unification with Taiwan."
But most Taiwanese businessmen were more upbeat.
"I'm very happy," said Jeffrey Hu, a Taiwan businessman who has been trading computers in Hong Kong for seven years. "There's nothing to worry about."
"It's good for Chinese to return to the Chinese fold," said the 58-year-old Taiwanese.
His sentiment was echoed 40-year-old Taiwanese interior designer Andy Lo, who has lived in the territory for five years.
"I feel quite good," Lo said. "A handover is quite good," he said, adding he was happy for Chinese people because the handover represented a reunification of China.
Lu Yen Wang, a Taiwan businessman who has been in Hong Kong for eight years, said he was moved by the handover ceremony.
"I attended the handover ceremony. It was touchy," said Wang. "This was a historic event."
Many Taiwanese businessmen in the territory were optimistic about their future under Chinese rule.
"It makes no difference to me. I'm here only to work, to do business," Lo said. "It's just as before."

Paul Lau, secretary-general at the Taiwan Businessman Association, agreed. "I believe many Taiwanese businessmen are optimistic," said Lau. "Many are staying in Hong Kong, without talking about leaving. They continue their business here."
"Many Taiwanese have direct investment in China. If they were worried about the issue of '97 (Chinese rule), then they wouldn't have invested in China directly," he said.
